lead: This unit teaches how machines assign categories to data. After reading, you can build and compare tree, probabilistic, distance‑based and margin classifiers and know when to use ensembles.
about: Unit 3 covers nine chapters that progress from simple rule trees to sophisticated probabilistic and geometric models. Chapter 3.1 introduces decision trees with ID3, entropy and information gain. Chapter 3.2 reviews Bayes theorem, MAP and maximum‑likelihood estimation. Chapter 3.3 builds the Naive Bayes classifier. Chapter 3.4 explains the Bayes optimal classifier and the Gibbs sampling trick. Chapter 3.5 presents Bayesian belief networks for structured probability. Chapter 3.6 describes k‑nearest neighbour and instance‑based learning. Chapter 3.7 covers support vector machines, maximum margin and kernel tricks. Chapter 3.8 adds ensemble methods such as bagging, boosting and random forests. Chapter 3.9 finishes with locally weighted regression, radial‑basis‑function networks and case‑based reasoning. Each chapter links to the next, reinforcing concepts and preparing you for the exam.

chapters.idea: Decision tree builds a classifier by splitting on attributes using information gain.
chapters.depth: Define entropy H = - Σ p_i log₂ p_i. Show information gain = H(parent) - Σ (N_child/N_parent) H(child). Explain ID3 steps: compute gain for each attribute, choose highest, recurse until pure or no attributes. Mention other names CART and C4.5 used in some syllabi.

figure.aria: Decision tree showing split on Outlook attribute with leaf classifications.

chapters.example: Weather data: 5 records – (Sunny, Hot, High, Weak, Play), (Sunny, Hot, High, Strong, No), (Rain, Mild, High, Weak, Play), (Rain, Cool, Normal, Strong, No), (Sunny, Mild, Normal, Weak, Play). Compute entropy of Play, then information gain for Outlook, and decide the first split.
chapters.trap: Forgetting to weight child entropy by the proportion of records leads to a wrong gain value.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 concepts of entropy and probability.
chapters.leave: Tree pruning, regression trees, and cost‑complexity pruning.

chapters.idea: Bayes theorem updates a prior with likelihood to give a posterior.
chapters.depth: Write P(C|X)=P(X|C)P(C)/P(X). Explain MAP selects class with max posterior and MLE selects parameters that maximize P(X|θ). Mention alternative name maximum a posteriori (MAP). Show how denominator cancels when comparing classes.

figure.aria: Block diagram showing prior and likelihood multiplied to produce posterior.

chapters.example: A biased coin is tossed 10 times and shows 7 heads. MLE bias = 7/10 = 0.7. With a uniform prior, MAP bias = (7+1)/(10+2) = 0.8.
chapters.trap: Using P(X) as a constant for each class but forgetting to cancel it when ranking classes gives wrong MAP values.
chapters.leave: Bayesian inference for continuous distributions and hierarchical models.

chapters.idea: Naive Bayes assumes feature independence to compute class posterior.
chapters.depth: Formula: P(C|X)=P(C)·∏_i P(x_i|C) / P(X). Explain training counts, Laplace smoothing, and variants: Gaussian NB for continuous, multinomial NB for text. Some syllabi call it Bayesian learning with independence assumption.

figure.aria: Block diagram showing prior and independent likelihoods multiplied to give posterior.

chapters.example: SMS spam detection: Vocabulary contains words "free" and "win". In spam messages, "free" appears 30 times, "win" 20 times out of 100 spam words. In ham messages, "free" appears 5 times, "win" 2 times out of 200 ham words. With Laplace smoothing, compute P(spam|"free","win").
chapters.trap: Skipping Laplace smoothing creates zero probability for unseen words and forces the whole product to zero.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 2 on Bayes theorem and MAP.
chapters.leave: Full Bayesian networks and exact inference algorithms.

chapters.idea: Bayes optimal classifier chooses the class with lowest expected loss under the posterior distribution.
chapters.depth: Define expected 0‑1 loss L = Σ_h P(h|D)·error(h). Show Bayes optimal error = min_y Σ_h P(h|D)·I[h(x)≠y]. Explain Gibbs algorithm: sample a hypothesis h from posterior and use its prediction. Some syllabi refer to it as Bayesian model averaging.

figure.aria: Directed graph showing two hypotheses weighted by posterior probabilities pointing to a combined prediction.

chapters.example: Two hypotheses for a binary task: h₁ predicts 0 with posterior 0.6, h₂ predicts 1 with posterior 0.4. Compute Bayes optimal error = 0.4 and Gibbs error = 0.5.
chapters.trap: Assuming Gibbs error equals Bayes optimal error; Gibbs is always higher or equal.
chapters.leave: Proof of error bounds and extensions to non‑0‑1 loss.

chapters.idea: Bayesian belief networks encode joint distributions with a directed acyclic graph.
chapters.depth: Define nodes as random variables, edges as direct dependencies, and conditional probability tables (CPT). Explain d‑separation for independence and variable elimination for inference. Some syllabi call them probabilistic graphical models.

figure.aria: Directed graph with Disease node pointing to Symptom node.

chapters.trap: Multiplying CPT entries without normalizing the result leads to probabilities >1.
chapters.leave: Learning network structure from data and approximate inference methods.

chapters.idea: k‑nearest neighbour classifies by majority vote of the k closest training points.
chapters.depth: Define Euclidean distance d = √ Σ (x_i - y_i)². Explain choice of k, weighted voting (e.g., 1/d), and Voronoi diagram interpretation. Some syllabi use term instance‑based learning.

figure.aria: Scatter plot showing two classes and a query point with its three nearest neighbours highlighted.

chapters.example: Points as in the plot. For k=3, compute distances from query (3,4) to all points, select three smallest, find two from Class B and one from Class A, assign class B.
chapters.trap: Using squared distance instead of square root changes the neighbour ordering when dimensions differ.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 distance metrics and basic geometry.

chapters.idea: Support vector machine finds the hyperplane with the largest margin between classes.
chapters.depth: Define margin and optimization: minimize ½‖w‖² subject to y_i (w·x_i + b) ≥ 1. Explain support vectors as points on the margin. Introduce kernel trick: replace dot product with K(x_i,x_j). Mention linear, polynomial and RBF kernels.

figure.aria: 2‑D plot showing two classes, the separating hyperplane and margin lines with support vectors.

chapters.example: For points (1,2) (+) and (-1,-1) (−), the hard‑margin SVM yields w = [1,1] and b = 0, giving decision function f(x)=x₁+x₂. Margin equals 1/‖w‖ = 0.71.
chapters.trap: Omitting bias term b when computing f(x) gives an offset error.
chapters.prereq: Linear algebra basics from Unit 1 and distance concepts from k‑NN.
chapters.leave: Soft‑margin formulation, SMO solver, and multi‑class SVM strategies.

chapters.idea: Ensembles combine several learners to reduce error and improve robustness.
chapters.depth: Explain bagging: train each base learner on a bootstrap sample, aggregate by majority vote. Describe random forest: bagging plus random feature selection at each split. Outline boosting (AdaBoost): maintain sample weights, train sequential learners, combine with weighted vote. Some syllabi refer to bootstrap aggregating as bagging.

figure.aria: Block diagram showing three decision trees feeding into a majority‑vote block.

chapters.example: Three trees predict classes: Tree1 → A, Tree2 → B, Tree3 → A. Majority vote gives final prediction A. For AdaBoost, after first round weights are updated: mis‑classified sample weight doubles, correctly classified weight halves; second learner focuses on harder samples.
chapters.trap: Assuming bagging reduces bias; it mainly reduces variance.
chapters.prereq: Decision tree chapter and k‑NN for distance weighting.
chapters.leave: Gradient boosting, stacking, and model‑averaging theory.

chapters.idea: Locally weighted regression fits a model using weighted nearby points, and RBF networks implement this with radial basis functions.
chapters.depth: Define weight w_i = exp(-‖x - x_i‖² /(2σ²)). Show weighted linear regression formulas for coefficients. Explain RBF network as Σ α_j φ(‖x - c_j‖) with φ Gaussian. Mention case‑based reasoning as retrieving similar past cases. Some syllabi call it instance‑based regression.

figure.aria: Plot showing data points and a query point at x=3 where nearby points receive higher weights.

chapters.example: Data as in the plot. Query x=3, σ=1. Compute weights: w₁=exp(-4/2)=0.14, w₂=exp(-1/2)=0.61, w₃=1, w₄=exp(-1/2)=0.61, w₅=exp(-4/2)=0.14. Perform weighted least squares to obtain local slope ≈0.9 and intercept ≈1.2, giving prediction y≈3.9 at x=3.
chapters.trap: Using unnormalized weights makes the regression coefficients too large.
chapters.prereq: Linear regression from Unit 2 and distance metric from k‑NN.
chapters.leave: Deep RBF networks and advanced kernel regression methods.
